author: Richard Eldred
title: News Round-Up
text:
- “
Jew hate ‘out of control’ in UK” – Israel says that antisemitic attacks are out of control in the UK after two Jewish men were stabbed in a terror attack in Golders Green, according to the Telegraph. - “
Police release body-worn footage of Golders Green arrest after terrorist incident declared” – The Met has released footage from the body-worn cameras of the responding officers to today’s attack. - “
‘Shame on you!’ Furious bystanders heckle Met chief Mark Rowley” – Sir Mark Rowley has been heckled with chants of “shame on you” and “resign” at the scene of the Golders Green terrorist attack, reports GB News. - “
This isn’t just a crisis for British Jews. It’s a crisis for Britain” – Eager to appease the extreme element of the Muslim vote, our politicians have taken sides, writes Nicole Lampert in the Telegraph. - “
Police raid Islamic sect over claims of rape and forced marriage” – Hundreds of officers have raided the Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light – a sect which relocated from Sweden to a former orphanage in Crewe in 2021 – following allegations of rape and forced marriage, reports the Mail. - “
Starmer firebomb suspects recruited by Russian speaker ‘El Money’, court hears” – Jurors at the Old Bailey have been told that three arson attacks on properties and a vehicle linked to Sir Keir Starmer were ordered by a Russian-speaking Telegram contact called “El Money”, who offered cryptocurrency as payment, says GB News. - “
Why is the Starmer arson trial being buried?” – When three men are accused of a coordinated campaign to torch properties linked to the sitting Prime Minister, and the nation’s editors collectively determine there are more pressing matters, we do not have a free press, writes Paul Knaggs in Labour Heartlands. - “
Starmer refuses to rule out sacking Reeves” – At the final PMQs before next week’s local elections, the Prime Minister refused to back his Chancellor when directly challenged by Kemi Badenoch, according to GB News. - “
Lord Hermer ‘committed treason’ with witch hunt against British troops” – Former security minister Tom Tugendhat has accused Lord Hermer of “treason” over his role in a notorious witch hunt against British troops, says the Telegraph. - “
The moral sickness poisoning Lord Hermer’s Britain” – A culture of legal impunity has left British soldiers facing prosecution while those who genuinely threaten the country have gone unchallenged, writes James Orr in the Telegraph. - “
The fall of Britain: a tragedy in three horrifying acts” – Fiscal collapse, radical ideology in government and a breakdown of national cohesion have combined to push Britain toward a crisis of historic proportions, warns Allister Heath as the columnist turns playwright in the Telegraph. - “
Nigel Farage opens door to Tory coalition” – The Reform UK leader has dramatically softened his stance on working with the Conservatives in marked contrast to last year when he flatly ruled out any pact, says the Telegraph. - “
Lib Dem election candidate wins legal challenge after being blocked from standing as MP due to Christian beliefs” – The Lib Dems have admitted to multiple counts of unlawful discrimination against former BBC journalist David Campanale in a landmark legal case expected to cost the party more than £250,000, reports GB News. - “
Illegal migration: between faith and scepticism” – On Substack, Dr David McGrogan examines small boat crossings as a semiotic act – a deliberate performance of vulnerability that shapes political and media responses before a single fact is established. - “
‘Come on in, there’s plenty of room’: the pro-migrant messages in children’s schoolbooks” – Children in more than a thousand schools are being fed pro-migration messaging through books featuring cartoon lions crossing the Channel in small boats, reports the Telegraph. - “
Iraqi who killed teen committed to psychiatric care in Germany” – A rejected asylum seeker who pushed a teenage girl to her death in front of a train in Germany has been committed to psychiatric care rather than prison, says the Mail. - “
Merz dared to challenge Trump. Now their relationship is in tatters” – Germany’s new Chancellor has paid a heavy price for openly defying Washington over the Iran war, writes James Rothwell in the Telegraph. - “
Endgame Timmy the Whale, endgame Merz the Pigeon Chancellor” – A humpback whale that has spent two months beaching itself off the German coast and stubbornly refusing to die is cast by Eugyppius on Substack as an unlikely metaphor for Friedrich Merz’s Chancellorship. - “
Iran’s cost of living is out of control as Trump’s blockade takes hold” – Trump’s naval blockade has been costing Iran an estimated £300 million a day, with shortages and surging prices now hitting ordinary Iranians, reports Akhtar Makoli in the Telegraph. - “
My takeaway from the WHCD? Dudes rock” – The White House Correspondents’ Dinner assassination attempt is recast by Suzy Weiss of the Free Press as a big night for the kind of stoic men who keep their heads when everyone else loses theirs. - “
Letby defence given boost by new scientific research” – Experts have argued that babies are frequently born with antibodies that naturally bind to insulin, potentially undermining a key plank of the prosecution case against Lucy Letby, says the Telegraph. - “
Two thirds of UK teenagers to have mental health problem by 2030” – A report has found that 51% of 15 to 19 year-olds already have a mental or behavioural disorder, with anxiety, depression and ADHD driving a trend that will climb to 64% by 2030, according to GB News. - “
NIH has removed world’s ‘foremost coronavirus biologist’ from all grants; UNC placed professor on leave” – Amid a broader reckoning with gain-of-function research, the National Institutes of Health has cut all funding to Ralph Baric, the world’s leading expert on coronavirus engineering, with his university placing him on leave, writes Paul D. Thacker on his Substack. - “
Australian excess deaths statistically significant” – New peer-reviewed work supports previous findings that COVID-19 vaccines likely contributed to Australia’s excess deaths in 2021, according to Dr Raphael Lataster on the Okay Then News Substack. - “
Support Dr Dean Patterson consultant cardiologist” – A fundraising appeal has been set up for suspended consultant cardiologist Dr Dean Patterson, who is appealing a GMC interim order after raising patient safety concerns. Donations are being sought to cover legal costs and living expenses during the proceedings. - “
Ed Miliband plumbs new depths in condemning BP” – In the Telegraph, Jeremy Warner accuses the Energy Secretary of rank opportunism for condemning BP’s profits while refusing to acknowledge that sky-high oil prices are a direct consequence of the Iran war his own Government helped precipitate. - “
Spain and Portugal mark one year since massive blackout, still no one held accountable” – A full year has passed since Spain and Portugal were plunged into darkness in an historic blackout, yet not a single politician or executive has resigned or been held responsible, notes Breitbart. - “
Climate science’s biggest shift in decades: IPCC’s RCP8.5 is officially dead” – The IPCC’s own scenario committee has officially scrapped the catastrophic RCP8.5 emissions pathway as implausible, upending decades of doom-laden projections, writes Roger Pielke Jr. on his Substack. - “
Oversupply of volatile solar energy leads to record negative prices!” – Solar energy has been flooding grids to such a degree that power prices have turned negative on multiple occasions, according to P. Gosselin on No Tricks Zone. - “
Co-op City: what it looks like when energy reality catches up to you” – New York’s largest residential co-op has been hit with soaring energy costs after mandated green upgrades, offering a vivid case study of what happens when Net Zero ideology collides with the bills that real people have to pay, says Francis Menton in Manhattan Contrarian. - “
Claim: only conservatives who don’t like liberals oppose climate action” – In Watts Up With That?, Eric Worrall discusses a study claiming conservative opposition to climate policy is driven more by dislike of liberals than by any principled objection. - “
Who the hell put the psychologists in charge?” – Behavioural scientists have been allowed to shape climate and public health policy to a degree that represents one of the defining institutional mistakes of the century, argues John Ridgway in CliScep. - “
Even mentioning J.K. Rowling’s name gets you cancelled by the pro-trans mob” – Kezia Dugdale, the new Chair of Stonewall, who didn’t even endorse J. K. Rowling’s views on gender is facing demands to retract a speech simply for mentioning her name – a new low for trans activist pressure campaigns, says Janet Murray in the Telegraph. - “
Nobody has ever made the truth go away by asking people to stop talking about it” – After her Commons speech on grooming gangs was censored online, Katie Lam warns Toby on the Free Speech Union podcast that the Online Safety Act is being used to stifle debate.
If you have any tips for inclusion in the round-up, email us here.
summary: - “ The moral sickness poisoning Lord Hermer’s Britain” – A culture of legal impunity has left British soldiers facing prosecution while those who genuinely threaten the country have gone unchallenged, writes James Orr in the Telegraph. - “ Nigel Farage opens door to Tory coalition” – The Reform UK leader has dramatically softened his stance on working with the Conservatives in marked contrast to last year when he flatly ruled out any pact, says the Telegraph.
